questions.q: How does a surface-code ancilla qubit extract its stabilizer's syndrome?
options: It is entangled via CNOT (or CZ) gates to its up to 4 neighboring data qubits, then measured -- the same primitive as chapter 3's 2-CNOT bit-flip code circuit, scaled up
It directly measures each neighboring data qubit one at a time
It uses a completely different mechanism unrelated to the small-code syndrome circuits from chapter 3
It requires cloning the neighboring data qubits before measurement
questions.explain: The same ancilla-entangle-then-measure primitive from lesson 13 is reused here, just with up to 4 CNOTs instead of 2, matching the surface code's 4-qubit stabilizers.

questions.q: Why does surface-code syndrome extraction run in parallel across the whole lattice rather than one stabilizer at a time?
options: Every stabilizer has its own dedicated ancilla, so all can be prepared, entangled, and measured simultaneously in the same timestep
Parallel extraction is impossible on real hardware and is only a theoretical idealization
Only one stabilizer on the entire lattice is ever measured per computation
Parallel extraction eliminates the need for ancilla qubits entirely
questions.explain: Because each lattice stabilizer has its own ancilla, measurement can happen simultaneously across the whole lattice, which is what makes the surface code practical on real multi-qubit hardware.

questions.q: Why can't the surface code rely on a single round of syndrome measurement, unlike how the small codes in chapter 3 were presented?
options: The surface code is meant to protect a logical qubit continuously, so faulty ancilla measurements must be distinguished from real errors by tracking patterns across many rounds over time
The surface code doesn't use ancilla qubits at all, making single-round measurement irrelevant
A single round of syndrome measurement is always sufficient and multiple rounds are purely redundant
Multiple rounds are only needed if the code distance is less than 5
questions.explain: Because the surface code runs continuously and ancilla measurements are themselves imperfect, repeated rounds let a decoder distinguish persistent real errors from isolated faulty measurement rounds.

questions.q: How does a real data error typically appear across multiple rounds of syndrome extraction, compared to a faulty ancilla measurement?
options: A real data error causes a stabilizer outcome to flip and stay flipped in subsequent rounds until corrected, while a faulty measurement typically causes just an isolated single-round flip
Both appear completely identically, and there is no way to distinguish them
A real data error only ever appears in the very first round and never afterward
A faulty measurement causes every stabilizer on the lattice to flip simultaneously
questions.explain: The persistence of a flipped outcome across rounds is the key signal distinguishing a genuine error from a one-off faulty measurement, which is exactly why tracking time matters.

questions.q: What is a 'defect' in the surface code's spacetime syndrome picture?
options: A stabilizer outcome that flips and persists across multiple rounds, treated as needing to be paired with another defect or the lattice boundary to identify the likely error
A permanently broken physical qubit that can never be used again
Any ancilla qubit that has never been measured
A stabilizer that never changes its outcome, ever
questions.explain: Defects are the persistent syndrome flips tracked across the lattice (space) and rounds (time), which decoding algorithms (next lesson) pair up to infer the most likely error chain.
